Absalon Pederssonn
ab'sah-lon pay'der-son
n. (Norwegian preacher, historian and diarist, 1528–1575; author of On the Kingdom of Norway and of the Bergen Diary)
From Hebrew Abshalom (H53), father of peace; the patronymic Pederssøn, son of Peder.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Absalon Pederssonn, commonly called Beyer, was the nephew and heir of Geble Pedersson, bishop of Bergen, and the most articulate Norwegian of the Reformation generation. He taught in the cathedral school, lectured and preached in the city, and wrote two works that survive: Om Norgis Rige, On the Kingdom of Norway, finished in 1567, which laments the decay of a kingdom once great and now a Danish province; and a diary of Bergen life kept for sixteen years, which is the best record of a Norwegian town in that century. He also helped burn the last of the cathedral's images. The dictionary records him because lament over a nation's decline is a biblical act when it is done the biblical way: honestly, without flattering the past, and ending in repentance rather than in grievance. Jeremiah's Lamentations begin with exactly Absalon's subject and exactly his tone: “How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!” (Lam 1:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to lament as to mourn, to bewail, to express sorrow; a chronicle as a historical account of facts in the order of time; and glory as praise, honour, splendour, brightness.

expand to see more

LAMENT, v.i. [L. lamentor.] To mourn; to weep or wail; to express sorrow; to bewail.

CHRONICLE, n. [Gr. time.] An historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.

GLORY, n. [L. gloria.] Praise ascribed in adoration; honor; splendor; brightness; magnificence.

SOLITARY, adj. [L. solitarius.] Living alone; retired; remote from society; also, lonely, destitute of company.

Key Scripture

Lam 1:1 — "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!"

Hag 2:3 — "Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory? and how do ye see it now? is it not in your eyes in comparison of it as nothing?"

Jer 6:16 — "Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein."

Psa 102:14 — "For thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof."

Modern Corruption

Bergen humanist and preacher; his 1567 lament for Norway and his sixteen-year town diary are the best Norwegian records of the age.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is nostalgia used as a substitute for repentance. A people that mourns its lost greatness while refusing to name the sins that lost it has only exchanged one vanity for another, and the lament becomes a grievance against neighbours, foreigners or the age. Absalon is not wholly clear of this; his book blames the Danes freely. But he also blames his countrymen, and that is what makes it a lament rather than a complaint.

The principle to recover is that the right response to decline is to ask for the old ways and then walk in them. Haggai put the comparison to the men who wept over the second temple, asking “Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory? and how do ye see it now?” (Hag 2:3), and then told them to build. Jeremiah gives the method and records the refusal in one verse: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16). And the psalmist marks the sign of a coming mercy, that “thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof” (Psa 102:14).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qinah (H7015), a lamentation; Hebrew nethibah (H5410), a path.

Hebrew qinah (H7015) — a dirge, a lamentation; Lamentations 1:1.

Hebrew nethibah (H5410) — a path, a trodden way; Jeremiah 6:16.

Hebrew badad (H910) — alone, solitary, isolated; Lamentations 1:1.

Hebrew kabod (H3519) — weight, honour, glory; Haggai 2:3.

Hebrew aphar (H6083) — dust, dry earth, rubble; Psalm 102:14.

Usage

"“How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!” (Lam 1:1) — On the Kingdom of Norway, finished 1567."

"“Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16) — sixteen years of the Bergen Diary."

"“thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof” (Psa 102:14) — nephew and heir of Bishop Geble Pedersson."
